outcome: The Erdős–Szekeres conjecture ES(n)=2^(n-2)+1 remains open in general (still unresolved for n=7 and above), but Baek and Balko (SoCG 2025) proved it for the class of 'decomposable' point sets, and separately proved a relaxed 'split k-gon' version tight at exactly 2^(k-2)+1 for all k; independently, a December 2025 preprint reports partial (non-exhaustive) SAT-solver progress toward the n=7 case (ES(7)=33) without completing it.
summary: The statement in scope is the general Erdős–Szekeres conjecture that ES(n)=2^(n-2)+1 for arbitrary n, still open at the general level (proved only for n≤6, via earlier SAT work by Szekeres–Peters and later Scheucher, all predating the frozen revision). Two lines of post-window work bear on it. (1) Jineon Baek and Martin Balko, 'The Erdős–Szekeres Conjecture Revisited' (SoCG 2025, LIPIcs vol. 332, article 13; also a Journal of Combinatorics 2025/2026 version), presented at SoCG in June 2025, prove the exact conjecture for 'decomposable' point sets — a restricted class of configurations including the classical Erdős–Szekeres cap/cup sets and Valtr's Horton sets — which is a genuine case of the stated problem (restriction to a subclass of point sets), so it counts as `partial` progress with direction `confirmed` (the conjectured bound holds on this restricted class). The same paper also proves that every set of at least 2^(k-2)+1 points (no three collinear) contains a 'split k-gon', a relaxed convex-position notion, and shows this threshold is tight; this is a genuinely different (weaker) statement about a different combinatorial object, so by §3.1 it is a related problem, not a case of the stated one, and does not itself move the classification, though it is worth recording as context. (2) Dumitru Bogdan's December 2025 preprint 'Notes on the 33-point Erdős–Szekeres problem' (arXiv:2512.24061, submitted 2025-12-30) targets ES(7)=33, the first open instance of the exact formula, using a SAT encoding (Kissat solver, ~16.67M clauses, ~578K variables) with convex-layer anchoring; it explicitly reports only UNSAT certificates for some anchored subfamilies, not a full resolution, and notes 'pronounced runtime variability' and heavy-tailed cost that 'currently dominates the computational effort' — so it is progress/incomplete, not a status-changing event by itself, and does not surpass the Baek–Balko decomposable-sets result as the decisive event. No AI system (LLM, ML model, or AI-driven proof search) is credited in either paper; both are SAT-solver/combinatorial-proof work, which under §6.2 is explicitly not AI involvement. A search for AI-driven mathematical proof-search systems touching Erdős problems (e.g. the 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search' paper, which lists 9 solved Erdős problems) found no mention of the Erdős–Szekeres conjecture or happy ending problem among their targets. I chose Baek–Balko's decomposable-sets result, dated to the SoCG 2025 conference (June 2025), as the decisive event because it is the most substantial genuine case-restriction of the stated conjecture that has been digested (peer-reviewed, published proceedings); the Bogdan SAT preprint is noted as further undigested, incomplete progress in the same direction.
competing_reading: One could argue the status should be `open` with `no_change_found` true, on the reading that 'decomposable sets' is itself a variant/related notion (a structural restriction defined ad hoc for the paper) rather than a natural 'case' of the conjecture in the sense of restricting to a geometrically meaningful subclass like convex position or a dimension. If decomposable sets are read as a bespoke technical construct rather than a case of 'arbitrary n', the correct classification would be `open`/`no_change_found` with the split k-gon and decomposable-set results relegated to context in the summary only. I judge the decomposable-sets result to satisfy the case test (it restricts the point sets quantified over, removing territory from the general statement) rather than changing the question, but the line is not sharp.
what_would_settle_it: A close reading of the Baek–Balko paper's definition of 'decomposable' point sets against whether it is a natural geometric restriction (making it a case) or an ad hoc technical device tailored to their proof technique (making it a variant); and whether ES(7)=33 is fully settled by either exhaustive SAT verification or a human-checked proof, which as of the December 2025 Bogdan preprint had not occurred.
